title: Homeowner directly identifies self during registration
description: During account registration, the homeowner provides identifying account details to the Home Hub, enabling direct identification of the individual behind the household account.
assumptions: Registration includes personal identifiers such as name, email address, phone number, or username tied to the homeowner.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-effort based on generic LINDDUN identification taxonomy; exact sub-node may differ in the canonical threat tree.

title: Enrollment data can link devices and account to the same household
description: By enrolling cameras and sensors together with the account, the homeowner shares a set of identifiers that can be linked to one another, allowing the Home Hub to associate multiple devices, sensors, and the homeowner with the same household profile.
assumptions: Enrollment transmits device identifiers, serial numbers, network identifiers, or similar metadata alongside account registration data.
uncertainty_note: Exact LINDDUN Pro sub-node may vary; linkage risk is clear even if the precise node id is approximate.

title: Registration and enrollment traffic may disclose sensitive household setup in transit
description: Data sent on this flow may reveal that a specific household is creating an account and enrolling cameras or sensors, disclosing the existence and composition of the home's security/monitoring setup if observed in transit.
assumptions: The flow carries device type, count, identifiers, or setup metadata, and an observer can access traffic metadata or contents.
uncertainty_note: Applies especially if transport protection or metadata minimization is weak; exact node id is approximate.

title: Home Hub may store excessive registration and device enrollment data
description: On receipt of registration and enrollment data, the Home Hub may collect or retain more personal and device information than necessary for account creation and device onboarding, increasing privacy impact.
assumptions: The Home Hub persists account details, device identifiers, configuration metadata, or telemetry beyond what is strictly needed for setup.
uncertainty_note: Threat depends on implementation choices for collection and retention; exact sub-node may differ.

title: Homeowner may be insufficiently informed about registration and enrollment processing
description: The Home Hub may not adequately inform the homeowner what personal data and device metadata are collected during account registration and device enrollment, for what purposes, and how long they are retained or shared.
assumptions: The setup flow lacks clear, timely privacy notices or layered explanations during onboarding.
uncertainty_note: Generic unawareness risk inferred from the onboarding flow; exact node id is approximate.

title: Registration and enrollment processing may occur without valid consent or other lawful basis
description: If the Home Hub processes personal data and device metadata for purposes beyond what is necessary for setup, without obtaining valid consent or establishing another lawful basis, the onboarding flow can create non-compliance risk.
assumptions: The system processes personal data subject to privacy regulation and may use the data for analytics, profiling, or secondary purposes.
uncertainty_note: Compliance obligations depend on jurisdiction and actual purposes; exact node id is approximate.

title: Observation of unlock-code entry reveals guest participation
description: The existence and timing of the Guest User's temporary access-code submission to the Home Hub can be observed at the flow level, revealing that a guest is currently attempting to access the home. Even without learning the code itself, observing this communication can disclose the guest's involvement or presence at the property.
assumptions: Assumes an attacker can observe the communication or physical/electronic signaling associated with code entry at the hub.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement from LINDDUN Detecting categories; exact sub-node may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Home Hub can identify the guest through the temporary access code
description: On receipt of the temporary access code, the Home Hub may be able to identify a specific guest if the code is unique per person or booking. The destination's processing of the code can therefore turn an ostensibly simple unlock action into identification of the individual using it.
assumptions: Assumes temporary codes are uniquely assigned to a guest, reservation, or household visitor rather than being shared anonymously.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree sub-node may differ depending on whether the code directly identifies a person or identifies them indirectly via account/booking linkage.

title: Home Hub can link repeated door-access events to the same guest
description: If the Home Hub stores or processes the temporary access code as a persistent unique token, multiple unlock attempts or visits can be linked together and associated with the same guest. This enables building a pattern of the guest's visits or behavior over time.
assumptions: Assumes the same temporary code is reused across multiple accesses or is retained in logs so repeated events can be correlated.
uncertainty_note: Best-judgement node selection; exact sub-node depends on the threat-tree granularity for linkability via unique credentials.

title: Guest may be unable to deny having used the temporary access code
description: If the Home Hub logs successful or failed code submissions together with timestamps, the resulting records can be used as evidence that the guest attempted or performed entry. This can reduce the guest's ability to plausibly deny participation in the access event.
assumptions: Assumes the hub keeps attributable audit logs of code entry attempts and those logs are retained or disclosed.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate; applicability depends on whether logs are attributable to a specific guest rather than merely to an anonymous code.

title: Stored access-attempt records reveal guest presence patterns
description: By processing and storing received temporary access codes with timestamps, the Home Hub can reveal when a guest was present, attempted entry, or was expected at the property. This exposes the guest's involvement in the system through destination-side side effects and records.
assumptions: Assumes the hub stores access attempts, success/failure status, or related event logs.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate and may map to a more specific detecting sub-node in another LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Guest may be unaware that code entry is logged or profiled
description: The guest may not be sufficiently informed that entering the temporary access code at the Home Hub results in logging, retention, or further analysis of their access behavior. This creates a privacy threat if the destination processes the data in ways that are not transparent to the guest.
assumptions: Assumes the system does not clearly notify guests about logging, retention, or downstream use of access events.
uncertainty_note: Best-judgement node selection; exact sub-node depends on the available unawareness taxonomy in the applied LINDDUN Pro tree.

title: Guest code may be processed beyond the expected access-control purpose
description: The Home Hub may use the temporary access code and associated event data for secondary purposes, such as occupancy analytics, behavior monitoring, or sharing with third parties, beyond the guest's expectation of simply unlocking the door. If such processing lacks an appropriate legal basis or exceeds the stated purpose, it creates non-compliance risk.
assumptions: Assumes the hub or connected services retain and reuse access-event data beyond immediate authentication and door control.
uncertainty_note: This is a generic non-compliance threat contingent on actual retention, reuse, notice, and legal basis; exact node id may vary by compliance taxonomy.

title: Sensor event records can link activities within the household
description: By writing motion, door, and other sensor events into a persistent local log, the Home Hub creates a record that can be correlated over time to link events to the same household, room, device, or occupant behavior pattern. Even if individual events seem innocuous, their accumulation enables linkage of routines and co-occurring activities.
assumptions: The event log stores timestamps and device/sensor identifiers, or otherwise preserves enough context to correlate entries over time.
uncertainty_note: Tree node chosen by best judgement; exact sub-node may vary depending on the project's threat-tree version.

title: Event contents may identify occupants or devices
description: The Home Hub's act of logging detailed motion/door/sensor events may make specific devices, rooms, or indirectly household members identifiable, especially when entries include precise timestamps, sensor IDs, room labels, or device names.
assumptions: Logged events include metadata such as sensor identifiers, location labels, or fine-grained timestamps.
uncertainty_note: Identification may be indirect rather than explicit if no names are stored.

title: Logged sensor events disclose in-home activities
description: Writing raw sensor events to the local event log discloses privacy-sensitive information about presence, movement, entry/exit, occupancy schedules, and daily routines. The disclosure risk exists because the source chooses to persist these events rather than minimizing or aggregating them before storage.
assumptions: The events are stored with sufficient granularity to reveal behavior patterns.
uncertainty_note: Exact disclosure impact depends on retention period and event granularity.

title: Persistent storage in the local event log enables later disclosure
description: Once received by the Local Event Log, the data store may retain and expose historical sensor events to anyone or any component with access, enabling disclosure of long-term behavioral patterns beyond the immediate operational need.
assumptions: The data store retains events for some period and can be queried or accessed later.
uncertainty_note: This is a destination-side disclosure threat based on storage/retention behavior; exact applicability depends on access controls and retention settings.

title: The local log may store events without user awareness
description: If the Local Event Log stores motion, door, and sensor events without clear visibility to residents, they may be unaware that detailed behavioral data is being retained locally, undermining transparency.
assumptions: Residents are not clearly informed in the interface or documentation that these events are logged and retained.
uncertainty_note: Applies only if logging is not made sufficiently visible to affected users.

title: Retention of sensor events may exceed user expectations or consent
description: The Local Event Log may process and retain household sensor events for longer, or for broader purposes such as diagnostics or analytics, than users expect or have consented to, creating a non-compliance risk.
assumptions: There are stated privacy preferences, consent choices, or legal/policy constraints governing event retention or purpose limitation.
uncertainty_note: Compliance depends on the system's stated purposes, jurisdiction, and consent model; this threat is plausible but context-dependent.

title: Uploading raw camera clips discloses highly sensitive in-home activity to a third party
description: The Home Hub sends recorded camera footage from inside the home to cloud storage. This act of sharing can disclose occupants, visitors, routines, possessions, and activities to the cloud provider beyond what is strictly local to the home.
assumptions: Camera clips contain identifiable people or household context and are not fully transformed to remove sensitive content before upload.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context only provided interaction applicability, not the detailed threat-tree nodes.

title: Upload traffic metadata can link clips to a specific household and behavior patterns
description: Even if clip contents are protected, the upload flow itself can expose metadata such as device identifiers, account identifiers, IP address, timing, frequency, clip size, and destination endpoint usage. This can allow linking multiple uploads to the same household and correlating them with occupancy or activity patterns.
assumptions: Network or service metadata is observable by intermediaries or the receiving service and remains associated with a stable device/account.
uncertainty_note: Exact LINDDUN Pro sub-node may differ; using a generic linking node due to missing detailed tree in the provided context.

title: Upload metadata can identify the household or residents
description: Identifiers carried in transit, such as account tokens, device serials, IP address, or customer-specific endpoints, may directly or indirectly identify the household associated with the camera clips.
assumptions: The flow includes stable identifiers or network metadata that can be tied to a subscriber, address, or household.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree node id is approximate because the detailed LINDDUN Pro tree was not included in the retrieved context.

title: Cloud storage can expose clip contents to provider personnel or secondary processing
description: Once received, the cloud video storage environment may store, index, scan, or otherwise process the clips in ways that reveal private in-home activities to administrators, operators, or integrated services.
assumptions: The destination environment permits human or automated access beyond the minimum needed for storage and security operations.
uncertainty_note: Threat applies at the destination based on typical cloud-storage processing; exact internal practices are not specified.

title: Stored clips may be used beyond the original home-security purpose
description: After upload, the cloud storage service may retain and use the clips for analytics, service improvement, law-enforcement response workflows, model training, or other secondary purposes not expected by the household.
assumptions: The service terms or backend architecture allow secondary use or broad internal reuse of uploaded footage.
uncertainty_note: Purpose creep is a common destination-side detectability/content-awareness issue in privacy modeling, but the exact LINDDUN Pro node id is approximate.

title: Cloud retention and processing may be insufficiently transparent to users
description: Users may not be adequately informed about how long clips are stored, who can access them, whether they are analyzed, and under what conditions they are shared onward. This creates an unawareness threat at the destination.
assumptions: The service does not provide clear, timely, and specific notice about storage, retention, access, and downstream use of uploaded clips.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is best-effort due to lack of detailed threat-tree excerpts in the provided context.

title: Cloud storage of home video may occur without valid or sufficiently granular consent
description: The destination may receive and retain clips under bundled or unclear consent, or without meaningful consent from all recorded individuals such as visitors, household members, or bystanders captured by the camera.
assumptions: Consent is relied upon as a legal basis or user expectation, and recorded individuals are not all directly able to provide or manage that consent.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on jurisdiction and legal basis; included because home video commonly captures third parties who have not directly consented.

title: Home Hub may disclose more motion-alert data than necessary to the backend
description: When forwarding a real-time motion alert, the Home Hub may include excessive personal data beyond what is strictly needed for alert handling, such as precise timestamps, device identifiers, household identifiers, sensor history, or contextual metadata. This creates an avoidable disclosure from the source to another party in the system.
assumptions: The motion alert concerns activity in a home and therefore constitutes personal data or data relating to identifiable occupants. The backend does not need all possible accompanying metadata for its purpose.

title: In-transit alert metadata may disclose occupancy patterns
description: Even if the payload is limited, the flow of real-time motion alerts can disclose sensitive personal information through metadata such as timing, frequency, routing, and association between the Home Hub and backend account. Observing this flow could reveal presence at home, routines, or unusual activity patterns.
assumptions: An observer of the communication path, logs, or network metadata can access at least some flow metadata. Repeated motion alerts correlate with household behavior.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node selection is approximate because the retrieved context only explicitly mentions Dd.4 at a high level; this threat is grounded in implicit disclosure via metadata on the flow.

title: Backend receipt may expose motion alerts to more parties or systems than necessary
description: Once the backend receives the motion alert, it may process, replicate, log, or make it accessible to internal services, operators, analytics components, or third parties beyond what is necessary to deliver the mobile alert. This increases the set of involved parties exposed to sensitive household activity data.
assumptions: The backend stores or forwards received alerts to supporting components or personnel, and access is broader than strictly required for the service purpose.

title: Real-time motion alerts on this flow can link repeated events to the same household or user account
description: Because alerts originate from a specific Home Hub and are sent to a specific backend context, repeated transmissions may be linkable to the same household, device, or account over time. This enables building a behavioral profile of occupants based on correlated alert events.
assumptions: The flow carries stable identifiers or otherwise consistent metadata that lets events be associated with the same source or account over time.
uncertainty_note: The exact LINDDUN Pro subtree identifier for linkability is not present in the retrieved context; L.1 is used as best judgement.

title: Motion-alert transmissions may identify a specific household or occupant
description: Identifiers in the alert or its transport metadata, such as hub ID, account ID, IP address, or address-linked installation data, may allow the backend or an observer with auxiliary knowledge to identify the household or infer the identity of occupants associated with the motion event.
assumptions: The system uses identifiers or network information that can be tied to a natural person or household.
uncertainty_note: The exact identifiability subtree identifier is not provided in the retrieved context; I.1 is used as best judgement.

title: Real-time motion alerts may allow inference of sensitive household activities
description: The content and timing of motion alerts can reveal whether people are home, awake, moving between rooms, away on vacation, or following regular routines. Even without explicit identity fields, these alerts can enable inference of sensitive facts about private life.
assumptions: Motion alerts are sufficiently granular or frequent to support inference about behavior or occupancy.
uncertainty_note: The exact detectability/discoverability subtree identifier is not present in the retrieved context; D.1 is used as best judgement for inference/discoverability risk.

title: Notification content discloses occupancy/activity information
description: By pushing a motion-detected alert, the backend shares personal information about activity at the home. Even a brief message such as 'Motion detected' can disclose that the household is currently occupied, active, or being monitored, which is privacy-sensitive contextual information.
assumptions: Assumes the notification contains or implies that motion was detected at the homeowner's property and is sent without strong minimization of content.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-effort based on generic disclosure-by-sharing; exact sub-node may vary by the project's threat-tree version.

title: Push-notification metadata can link homeowner, device, and property events
description: Metadata on the notification flow, such as device token, account identifier, timing, and repeated event patterns, can enable linking of multiple motion events to the same homeowner or household over time, even if payload content is minimized or encrypted.
assumptions: Assumes standard mobile push infrastructure uses stable device/account identifiers and observable timing metadata.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node granularity may differ; this is a standard linkability risk on notification channels.

title: Notification traffic may identify the homeowner as a user of a home-security service
description: The existence, routing, or recognizable characteristics of the push notification may allow intermediaries or observers to identify the recipient as the user of a specific home-monitoring application or as the occupant of a monitored property.
assumptions: Assumes some party on the path or push ecosystem can observe app identity, endpoint metadata, or distinctive traffic patterns.
uncertainty_note: Applies mainly where push-service or network metadata is visible; payload encryption alone may not remove this risk.

title: Notification content or previews may disclose sensitive event details in transit or at intermediaries
description: If the notification includes detailed text, images, or location/context, those details may be exposed to push-service providers, OS notification services, lock-screen previews, or other intermediaries handling the message, causing disclosure beyond the intended recipient.
assumptions: Assumes notification payload or preview text contains event details and that intermediary services process or store notification data.
uncertainty_note: Some platforms encrypt parts of notification content; risk depends on implementation and notification design.

title: Notification may be exposed on the homeowner's device to unintended viewers
description: On receipt, the notification can be displayed on the lock screen, wearable, shared device, or notification history, disclosing that motion was detected at the home to family members, visitors, coworkers, or thieves with visual access to the device.
assumptions: Assumes device notification previews/history are enabled or the device is accessible to others.
uncertainty_note: This is a destination-side disclosure risk caused by how the external entity's device presents received data.

title: Homeowner may be unaware of notification visibility and downstream exposure
description: The recipient may not understand that motion alerts can appear on lock screens, companion devices, or be retained in notification logs, reducing predictability and user awareness about who can see the alert and when.
assumptions: Assumes the system does not clearly explain notification-channel privacy implications or provide granular controls.
uncertainty_note: Best-effort usability/privacy mapping; exact sub-node may vary across LINDDUN Pro versions.

title: Backend may send motion alerts without sufficiently specific consent or preference control
description: Sending motion-detected push notifications may exceed the homeowner's expectations or chosen preferences if consent for this category, timing, or level of detail was not explicitly obtained or cannot be managed, creating a non-compliance risk.
assumptions: Assumes notification preferences, lawful basis, or consent granularity may be insufficiently captured or enforced.
uncertainty_note: Compliance depends heavily on jurisdiction and product settings; included as a plausible risk rather than a certain defect.

title: Backend shares analytics that may still be linkable to individual users or devices
description: Although described as aggregated device-usage analytics, the backend's act of disclosing usage metrics to the analytics vendor can enable linking records to the same device, account, cohort, or household if aggregation is too granular, stable identifiers are retained, or repeated exports allow reconstruction over time.
assumptions: Assumes the shared analytics may include persistent pseudonymous identifiers, fine-grained cohorts, timestamps, or dimensions that permit singling out/linking across uploads.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context only confirms applicable threat types/positions, not detailed node ids.

title: Aggregated analytics may still permit identification of users or devices
description: If the backend shares small-cell aggregates, rare usage patterns, quasi-identifiers, or longitudinal metrics, the recipient may be able to infer the identity of a user, device, or other data subject behind the analytics.
assumptions: Assumes aggregation thresholds, k-anonymity-style controls, or suppression/generalization may be insufficient.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree node id may differ in the canonical LINDDUN Pro tree; selected by best judgement.

title: Disclosure risk from sharing analytics with a third-party vendor
description: The backend discloses device-usage analytics to an external analytics vendor. Even if aggregated, the transfer expands access to behavioral information and may reveal sensitive patterns about users, segments, or protected groups.
assumptions: Assumes the analytics contain behavioral or potentially sensitive usage information and are not fully anonymized beyond realistic re-identification/inference risk.
uncertainty_note: Detailed node id is approximate due to limited retrieved tree detail.

title: Vendor may further disclose or repurpose received analytics
description: Once the cloud analytics vendor receives the analytics, it may expose them internally, combine them with other customer datasets, or share them onward with subprocessors or affiliates, causing additional disclosure beyond the original expectation.
assumptions: Assumes vendor-side access controls, contractual restrictions, or onward-transfer limitations may be incomplete.
uncertainty_note: Applies if the vendor has broad processing/sharing rights; exact node id is best-effort.

title: Secondary use by the analytics vendor beyond the original purpose
description: The vendor may use the received analytics for purposes beyond providing analytics services, such as product improvement, benchmarking, model training, profiling, or cross-client insights, making the processing unexpected for data subjects.
assumptions: Assumes contractual terms or privacy notices do not strictly limit processing to the original analytics purpose.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; the underlying threat applicability is stronger than the exact citation.

title: Sharing analytics with the vendor may be incompatible with consent or notice
description: If users were not clearly informed that their device-usage analytics would be shared with an external cloud analytics vendor, or if no valid legal basis covers this transfer, the backend's disclosure may violate consent, transparency, or purpose-limitation requirements.
assumptions: Assumes the system relies on consent, legitimate interests, or another legal basis that may not adequately cover third-party analytics sharing.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is best-effort; compliance assessment depends on jurisdiction and actual notices/legal basis.

title: Vendor processing may not comply with contractual or regulatory constraints
description: The analytics vendor's receipt, retention, international transfer, or onward processing of the analytics may fail to meet applicable data-processing agreement terms, cross-border transfer rules, retention limits, or processor obligations.
assumptions: Assumes the vendor acts as processor/service provider or otherwise is subject to contractual and regulatory privacy obligations.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate and depends on the governing legal/regulatory regime.

title: Flow metadata may enable linking between backend activity and vendor datasets
description: Even if payload contents are aggregated, metadata on the transfer itself—such as timing, frequency, tenant identifiers, API keys, endpoint paths, or batch structure—can help link uploads to specific apps, cohorts, campaigns, or recurring populations.
assumptions: Assumes network/application-layer metadata is observable or retained by intermediaries or the vendor.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate.

title: Analytics may be exposed in transit if the transfer is insufficiently protected
description: If the backend-to-vendor transfer lacks strong transport security, certificate validation, or secure API handling, the analytics payload or sensitive metadata could be intercepted or exposed during transmission.
assumptions: Assumes transport protections may be misconfigured, downgraded, or bypassed; if robust TLS and endpoint authentication are enforced, likelihood is lower.
uncertainty_note: This is a genuine in-transit disclosure threat, but applicability depends on actual transport-security controls.

title: Linkability via retrieval metadata on the video-fetch flow
description: The retrieval flow can expose metadata such as homeowner account identifier, device/app identifier, clip identifier, timestamps, IP address, and access patterns. Observers of the flow or intermediaries could correlate repeated fetches to the same user, household, camera, or event, linking multiple playback actions and possibly linking them with other datasets.
assumptions: Applies if flow metadata is observable by network intermediaries, logs, analytics components, or other parties beyond what is strictly necessary.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-judgement because the retrieved context did not include the specific Linkability subtree for this interaction.

title: Identifiability of the homeowner through video retrieval traffic
description: Even if the video payload is protected, the act of retrieving a clip may reveal who is requesting it through identifiers in requests, authentication tokens, IP address, or distinctive timing and volume patterns. This can make the homeowner or household identifiable from the flow itself.
assumptions: Assumes request metadata or network characteristics can be observed or logged in identifiable form.
uncertainty_note: Specific tree-node citation is approximate; the general Identifiability threat clearly applies to observable request metadata.

title: Backend learns sensitive inferences from requested video clips
description: By receiving and processing requests for specific stored clips, the mobile app backend can infer sensitive information about the homeowner, such as presence at home, routines, incidents of interest, occupancy patterns, or security concerns, based on which clips are fetched and when.
assumptions: Assumes P2 has access to clip identifiers, timestamps, camera context, or playback history and can associate them with a user account.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-judgement; the exact Detectability/Disclosure subtree id was not provided in context.

title: Disclosure of video content or playback history at the backend
description: The backend receives highly sensitive personal data when retrieving stored video clips. If P2 stores, caches, logs, or otherwise exposes the clip content or associated playback history beyond what is necessary, unauthorized parties or internal actors could gain access to intimate household information.
assumptions: Applies if P2 can access plaintext video, thumbnails, derived metadata, or detailed access logs, and if controls are insufficient.
uncertainty_note: Specific subtree id is approximate, but disclosure of information at the destination is a strong fit for this flow.

title: Unawareness about backend retrieval and processing of stored videos
description: The homeowner may be unaware that the backend, rather than only the mobile app, retrieves and potentially processes, caches, or logs stored video clips and playback events. This can undermine transparency about who accesses the footage and for what purposes.
assumptions: Applies if notices, UI, or privacy documentation do not clearly explain backend-side retrieval, caching, logging, or secondary processing.
uncertainty_note: Tree node citation is approximate because the relevant Unawareness subtree was not included in the retrieved context.

title: Violation of storage limitation for retrieved clips or playback logs
description: After retrieving the stored video, the backend may retain cached copies, thumbnails, transcoded versions, or detailed playback/access logs longer than necessary for delivering playback. Retaining this personal data beyond necessity violates storage limitation obligations.
assumptions: Assumes P2 persists retrieved content or access logs and retention is not strictly limited to the playback purpose.
